div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 22, 1889.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 22, 1889.
THE JOHNSTOWN DISASTER.

Mm. Kitty,iif Llanidlom, has received a letter from her A., dated ohnstown. June 3. He fiats ° I lI4Ve headed the letter Johnstown, but Hod knows it is not much of n town, now ; there are only a few of the larg- est buildings left standing. There are some small vill- ages on the bill surnanaling the town all right, but the Natal is all ruined." The writer goes im to any riots when the reservoir burst the houses went past him like trains. Dimr timid.. were screaming and crying pitifully. 'My mite, I, and the two children got up into the attic, and our house then moved off. I stood with one of the children in my arms. and my wife stood by my aide with the other little one. In about three minutes we struck against the other houses at the bridge. Said I • Now jump, Lizzie, for your life: We both jumped with the children on to some two of wood on the river, and than climbsal to the nod of the house. When we got up Little's father and mother and sister and brother were there. We managed to climb over the , debris to <lry land and 'were saved. But all we owned In the noirld is gone.- The writer concludes by giving names of many PITS/MIS from Llatiiilloea saved, but says that Dick Worthington lost his wife and three children, and Moses Owen, both of Llanidloes, lus wife and sin children.

'rho folios ing parileulars-of of, disastrous fire, in which 150 men, women, and children are said to have perished at Akbarpore, sub-division Behar, have been sent to the "Statesman" by a correspondent. It appears there wean marriage in the house of a Itajput on April 28. As usual, there was a large gathering of br.til non es. While the ceremony wan being proceeded with a fire broke out at the entrance of the house, and as a strong westerly wind was blowingat thetime.theentire premises were enveloped in flames in the course of a few minutes. Some of the men managed to extricate themselves by rushing to the door. But the difficulty was how to save the women and children. The greatest confusion prevailed. (Inc Sipalli Singh, the father of the bride- groom and a brave Rajput, had the presence of mind to snatch his son and the bride from the crowd, and go- ing to the roof let therm down in a lane running close to the house, and told them to run for their lives. . flaying thus then reeollected that In. had lett a Ism of 150 rupees behind Idle,, he returned to the /lOUS. He recovered the bag, and was preparing to make his escape 'when he heard the lenient. tions of women and children proceeding from a nom, the door f..f which was shut. Sipabi was too brave and node a fellow to think of his personal safety when three helpless creatures were In imminent danger of being burned to death. Hi' opened the door, and the seene which followed defies description. The , females rushed out end laid hold of him, each one in despair calling out, "Save me, stve me!" He was a man of splendid physique, and if left alone might have suenieded iti saving some if not all : his what could the , poor Inure. against simany distracted WOMen and child- ren clinging tilniw fordear life ? He fella.n the ground,and they crowdeti round him. A few minutes more and the free had done its worst. Nothing was to be seen but a heap aif esarnsl remains. The police were on the spot after the ueident. and buried the dead in three wells of the village. The fire extended to other huts, and Akharpore inn wreck.

A CANADIAN TRAGEDY.

A SAII tragedy is reported Fran Canada. A fire broke out in ,00 tM. Wilson, a rest wetable eititen nf r, Ontario. The tunes spread with terrible rapidity, and Min. Wilson and two children were burned Ito death. Mr. Wilson hthaved with conspicuous lantry, and ...vetted in saving three other children. But he was terribly burned, and when he learned that, : despite his frantic efforts, there was no possibility : saving the I.st of his C. 'ly. he lost his reason.

A Frenchwoman named Brandin strangled her three. yearwld boy at 58. Pitt.st., Tottenham wrt-road, Lon - don, on Monday morning, and then strangled herself. The woman was married anti with her Inistund lodged in the house. A later report says the name of the deceased is Bruin, and her husband Joseph Drum. woo a dealer in curiosities. Ile found his wife and boy. dead on returning front his club early on Monday morning. It is stated that the dead woman had suspected her hus- band of infidelity. but Drum declared hdo wife had m., cause whatever for jealousy. On Wednesday an inquest was held on the bodies. div.head: MR. BALFOUR ON ROME RULE,
div.p: MR. BALFOUR ON ROME RULE,

Speaking on Wedne.lay night at the annual dinner of the Constitutional Union' held in London, Mr. A. J. Balfour, M.P., criticised Mr. tiladstone's recent utter- ances with regard to Ireland, and said they might be told that the ideal of government, self-governing munici- palities in um- free organii: state—which he, the Chief Secretary. had always held to be the right one—was impoasible m far its Ireland was cinleerllod. But if Irish sentiment was so fully opposed to sucha form of Govern- ment that they had no hope of establishing it upon a around permanent basis how could any stability he expected from such a compromise as Bane lisle ? friends of Ireland forgot what they ought to remember, and they remembered when they ought to forget. They strove to stir up animosity and discontent by ever drag- ging forward Ireland's wrongs, and never referring to what hail been done for her amelioration. Yet l'lster WAR satisfied with the Union. and the Conservative and Unionist party desired that Ulster should have a share in the Empire. Nay, they hoped to knit every class awl creed in Ireland ch., together and to the Union, and not all the forces of disintegration, allied though those forces might be with treason and crime, should make the present Government fail in the aim that they had set ' -v. themselves.

div.head: NONCONFORMISTS AT CAMBRIDGE.
div.p: NONCONFORMISTS AT CAMBRIDGE.
bf.re

Mr. J. Carvell Williams writing to the '• Daily News!' says t—Lust year the Senior Wrangler at Cambridge was a Nonconformist, and so was the second on the list. This year the seine thing has again happened ; only the second name is hracketted with another. This is more than a mere coincidence U it is in accordance with the COllll4. of academic events in Cambridge during the last thirty years, Nonconformists having appearol at the top of the list no fewer than nineteen times! Here is the list of the years, vie., 1860, 1161, 1862, 1866, 1867, 1868, 1869, 1871, 1873, 1875, 1877, 1879, 1880, 1881, 1882, 1885, 1886, 1888—from which it will be ustn that at two periods a Nonconfonnist occupied the position for four years in succeasion, and at another period for three years in suecession. And—to say nothing of the past—l inav add that this year other Nonconformists stand very high up in the inathernatical tripos list. It was Mr. James fleywaxl who struck the first successful blow at ecelesiastical exclusiveness at the Universities, when in 1854 lie earried a fiA UM` in the Oxford University Reform Rill abolishing the ecclesiastical tests which had practic- ally shut Dissenters out of Oxford. lam glad that in his old age he witneases such results of his and ether men's labours to make cant Universities national in fact, as well as name; and I hope that younger men will see to it that before long ecclesiastical tests eon' tO h. unposed in in other National Educational Institutions in which they still exist.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE'S CAMPAIGN.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S CAMPAIGN.

Mr. Gladstone arrived at Poole, on Saturday, from Plymouth. At the Ladies Walking Ground, a great cm cif had aasemblisl, and the right hon. gentleman, having been presented with an address by the local Libensls, refernsl„ in the course of a brief reply, to the sugar bounties I itiestion, and expressed the hope that the example set by seine courageous Tories would make the Dissentient Liberals pluck no isiurage to aive on this single occasion a vote on the side of liberty and against restriction. lievertingto the Irish I westion. he said that the strength of a eountry was found in the attachment of the people, which gave rise to patriotic energies, and these patriotic energies reachisi the MMXiMIIIII when exercised by a people who were of one mind. After- wards, on passing through Wiinborne, Mr. I iLadstone spoke for a few minutes in acknowledgment of an address from the local Liberals. At Blandford, Mr. Gladstone received an adder., from the North Dorset Liberal Association, hut as rain was falling at the time Mr. Gladstone confined his remarks to a few sentences, and proceed.] by coach to lwerne, the seat of Lord Wolverton, when lie spent Sunday. On Monday Mr. Gladstone completed his Whitsuntide tour in the West of England, mid returned to London and to his place in the House of Commons, on its meet- ing after the teem. In the morning Mr. Gladstone drove from Lord Wolverton's wet jet Irwene, through Shaftesbury, to tilillingham' where lie joinettan express , train which was stopped for him, and proctvded to London. At Shaftc,bury he received an address, and in the course of his reply said the franchise would become a reoekery and a delusion if the people did not vote according to their convictions. There were grave sus- picions that the Primrose League was a boycotting asaoriation, but he hoped the Liberal party would not try to influence votes either by fear or favour. At fill- linghatn, Mr. Gladatene referred to the land question as affecting agricultural labourers, and said it would he a serious public calamity if the rural population were diminishol by emigration or ether mean,. Ile urged that the way to main this population was to give them an opportunity of attaching themselves to the land, and the cultivation of the plots of land by agricultural labourers would benefit both the 'labourer and the far- mer. When the train reached Salisbury Mr. Gladstone nude another brief speech from the carriage window, land eventm-lly arrived St Wagorloo Station at about three o'clock, and at tke Douse of Commons at half- pun three.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOHN TINSLEY.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOHN TINSLEY.

The death occurred, on Wedn..stlay evening, of Mr. John Tinsley, of Birchfield, lirappenhall, and a member of the firm of Messrs. John and James Tinsley. tanners, Mersey-at., Warrington. About a fortnight ago the deceased gentleman .was attacked with illness, but an improvement in his condition took place. It was, however, followed by a relapse, which resulted in the death of Mr. Tinsley from rheumatic gout, at the age of 61 years. The deceased gentleman and his brother com- menced business in a small way in Mersey- st., and the operations of the firm gradually increased until the business obtained its pre- sent. large dimenaions. .Mr. John Tinsley took a prominent part in ecclesiastical affairs, and was a vice-president of the English Church Union. Ile was a staunch Conservative and gave active support to the Tory party in Warrington and also in Cheshire. Ile was a member of the Primrose League, was on the Management Committee of the Warrington Clergy Daughters Institution,and was a trustee of the Warrington Blue Coat School. The deceased gentleman. who was a widower, and who leaves two children to ninum his loss, was in his illness attended by Dr. Leach, of Manchester, and by Dr. Starkey Smith, of Warrington. The deceased gentleman was at business no later than a fortnight ago, when he appeared to be in excellent health, anti about that time attended a Committee meeting at the Conservative Club in Sankey-at. in his caps- city as treasurer. Par some years he had suffered . from gout, but when symptoms indicated that the ' disease had spread to his head, his condition became serious, and caused his friends great anxiety. The funeral will take place on Saturday morning in Orappenhall churchyard. On Thursday evening, at a meeting of the Warrington Habitation of the l'rimrose League, a resolution of condolence with the bereaved relatives was passed.

Titr. .influct of the Government Clliilying M dealing with the Sugar Bounties Bill is reprehensible in the highest degree. They will neither go forward with it nor give it up and own that they have inado a mistake. They took to themselves credit for having moved in the matter in the first instance ; for they were reeler the impression that , this particular nit of Protection would be accepted ES a :0.14 morsel by the working classes. But monopolists sought to reap where the Ministry had NAM ; sugar increased in price at the hare prospect 11l the passing of the Sugar lkiuntiea Bill : and in the meantime it has been made tl derably dear that the eonntry will have none of it The bill should have been dealt with before the Whitsuntide recess, DT withdrawn altogether, but Mr. Smrntin answer to question after question, intimated that it would be taken after the holidays. The holi- days are ricer, and now we are told that "tine lovernment do riot think it necessary tnn press for the consideration of the measure this year. That is to say, the bill is to be dropped for the present session; for anything that anybody knows to the con- trary, it may lie reintrothmal next ymtr. It is suggestive that Mr. GLADSTONE SIDSIM 1101101111e0 LllO measure OD Saturday, and dint MY. SMITH Phollid niH Mf ,mlay make this humiliating announcement. But why, if the Government find that they have blundered in this matter, and that they cannot Ismail° bill at all, do they not admit ' that it is dead, mid sweep it out of the way with other rubbish Is it that they want to let them- selves town easy, or are they really so infatuated •as to suppose that a measure which is detested this year will next year be welcomed with open arms. Speaking at Rochester, on Tuesday even- ing, and referring to their action, Lord Grauville said :

They are sitting on *fence, to tho great detriment of present trade, in the mat t erof the Sugar Bounties Convention, 6 nvasure which appears to me to he oppowul to political economy, injurious to the goal administration of the Customs, nj 11110 n., to the free- trim of trade. as well as a deprivation to the con- sumer of what has Ituveno a necessary of life Btheors)---and injurious to certain industries which flourish more particularly in Kent --(cheers) -and lastly, they 1•XP0.,13 to very (lati4erois risks in oar intereMonial nut internal, mal relations. (Cheers.)

This puts the case in a nut-shell, and it is a case which is strong against the Government. All • the trades which are dependent upon sugar have suffered already by the commercial dis- turbance which the Sugar Conventimi has muted. If Parliament is really possessed of so ranch midsummer madness :is to set up a boycott and make sogar dearer, let 118 as soon as 'seeable know the worst, atml make the best if a bail job. But this shilly-shallying is unstatcsmandike, tantalis- ing. and mischievous. It looks as if the Ministry Ii tint rare a straw 1111 W much trade might be deranged, providing they can be permitted to delay an acknowledgment of defeat. A Wigan collier named James Law, who came to Warrington on Monday to join the militia training, got Vs, much drink and was bolted up. Ile was brought before the magistrates on the morning of the following day, when evidence was given to the effect that on Mon- day evening he 1.-loved in a very disorderly manner on Pinner's-brow, striking everyone who came near him. After a hard struggle he was taken into custody and locked up. PS'. Singleton said that the crowd that as- semblol threw stones at the police, and '• hooted at them shamefully." One publican in the neighbourlexal was obliged to lock op his house ha' a considerable time,owing to the conduct of the prisoner and other militiamen who had come up bar training. The people there were hemming no lawless that they would et en attack the soldiers. The prisoner cal- culated upon someone rescuing him. Total WARRINGTON V. LIVRRPOOI..—The Warringtonians paid their annual visit to the Aighurth enclosure on Saturday afternoon. The weather was dull, but, fortunately, the rain kept off and a capital afternoon's cricket was.: wit- nosed. The Warrington team, it illicit he admitted, went decidedly lucky in making a draw of the match, as time alone prevented the Liverpudlians administering a cnishing defeat. The wicket WRS in fine order, and on winning the toss the Liverpool captain opened the inn- ings, A. T. Kemble and Price opposing the deliveries of Smith and Jolley. Runs came loot, mostly off the bat of the amateur, when at 27 he was smartly taken by Rey- nolds. With Outwore unaltcrol, the Roy. R. M. Ainslie put one up to Igiwton, which was saicly held. but when DinaglAs Steel and Price becanot associateil a protracted stand was made, the bgal bong advanced to one short of the eentury before a separation was effected. Mr. Steel had done the bulk of the hinting, his cutting being particularly fine. Included in his 54 Were eight fours, Hulse threes, and four twos. Four runs later, after playing very patiently for 15. Price was bowled. 11. R. Parr did not gave much [noble, but Mr. Nicholsin hit away in merry style. 11. F.. R. Harrison nude a good partner, hitting up 15, but following his dismissal the innings speedily came to a conclosion for 212. Mr. Nicholson carried out his bat for is grandly-played 75, included in his hits being one six (clean out of the ground), one five, seven fours, four tiirees, and seven twos. Of the Warrington bowlers, C. G. Lawton, who obtained three wickets for 37, and T. Jolley, three for 31, were most successful, Smith proving rather espen- rive, his four costing 97 runs. Warrington opened their defence with J. J. Cmsfield and Itaynolds, D. Q. Steel and Price sharing the bowling. The start was disarc trous, three wickets falling for nine runs. Messrs. Law- ton and R. Smith, however, stopped the "rut," and carried the won) to 36, when the former was taken be- hind the wicket. J. Annstiong and Smith advancrn the total to 57, when the former and Faulkner (the next comer) were smartly taken hi the slips from successive these being two really fine catches by Douglas Steel. The wickets again fell rapidly, hat" time" came to the relief of the Warringtonians, and the game ended in a draw, much to the satisfaction of the visitors. It. C. Harrison took three wickets for seven rims, and Price four for 21. Score.—

BURNLEY GAZETTE, February 23rd.

GIIE lot of those who toil from day to day in the bowels of the earth is not a very agreeable one. Apart from the terrible risks of which we are so often reminded by a calamitous explosion, with all its thrilling scenes, the collier has to pursue his work at _

times under circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowles, of 109, Oxford Road, Burnley-, has had some experience of the trying conditions of labour in some of the deeper coal mines of this country. Ile relates how he has repeatedly had to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water and the cold liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such conditions of employment are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has had to encounter them in other mining sufferer in consequence. He first commenced with pains in his head, which gradually extended to other parts of the body. ° " I got so low," said Mr. Knowles, with blankets and have a chair close to the fire even on a warm day. It was only then that I could feel anything like warmth. My legs got so weak that I had to have the help of a stick to get across the floor. I was terribly troubled with indiges- tion, nervous debility, and disease of the liver and kidneys, and had constant attacks of ciltinp in the stomach. For many weeks I suffered dreadfully, writhing in agony for hours together, and got so weak that it was painful to speak, let alone trying to move. Medico 'll seemed to make me worse, and I got so that my friends gave me ill and the doctor ventured to offer no hope of a cure. At last I read one of 'Warner's pamphlets, sent for a bottle of Wanier's SA} Cure,' and oh! how much good it did me. In n few weeks I was new man. My appetite returned, the weakness disappeared, and went back to my work feeling stronger than 1 had done for years.

SUICIDE OF A CHIEF CONSTABLE.

An Mnuest was held at Belgmve, Lei-ester, on Tues- day evening, on Captain Orimston, chief constable of Leicestershire, who committed suicide on Tuesday morn- ing. The evidence AlOWed that he had been under medical treatment for ill-health and depression, and had just returned after a short leave of absence. (In Monday morning he was found locked in a rocni. On the door being openol he was discovered dead, shot through the mouth. A revolver, one chamber of which was dis- charged, was lying at his feet. A verdict of suicide I during temporary insanity was returned. Deceased was much respected. He had bets, captain in the 93rd High- landers, adjutant of Volunteers, and became chief con- stable in 1876.

The betting nuisance is a strong element in producing poverty, u.s nanny spoor family will find out before these lines reach your readers when the husband and father will have taken his mrnings to the Manchmter race ' coume, or have deposited with some shark of a book- maker who has backed for the poor dupe the wrong horse and sent him borne penniless to a hungry family. The drink shop is responsible for the most of this tinn. The infettrrn- neglect or maladministration of the land is another great muse of our national poverty. It is an repas Tree with many rotten branches ) among them mar be mentioned the law if primogeniture, the law of I enMil, and the law of tithe.. The two former tend to ! keep the land inn few hands, and it becomes a monopole. I preventing the introduction of capital in the soddnaking ! the tenant farmer and the agricultural labourer the bond I slaves of the landlord, driving them from the soil into I the towns to compete with an already over-glutted , labour market. The land is untillcd and unproductive— barren for lark of a fertiliser, while the fertilising material of the towns becomes a nuisance, and Corpom- lions are at their wits ends to know how to dispose of it, and have to expend large sums in tip-rooms and other ways, in disposing of their sewage. rntil our land laws are based on common-sense, and on a footing with the laws which regulate our commerce, and until the olrl relics of feudalism are swept away, and we have free trade in land, with security for capital, we shall have I poverty. The emigration remedy will not effect a eta,. if we send awry men who should bp cultivating the land here and they go to countries when, land can be had for next to nothing—with taxes merely nominal—and they cultivate the land, having but little to pay elmpt for labour and their personal expenses. The White Star steamer Britannic, which arrived off Queenstown on Thursday. brings news of the total loss lot the British steamer Alt.-ire and the drowning of several passengers and seven of the crew, inelnding Mr. Turnbull, chief officer. She struek, on Aprill 22nd, on a dangerous restf sdf the Fiji Islands. The lifeboats were launched, and one loot's crew was prevented from landing by the natives. The captain and the rest of the new were pieked up lit a passing steamer, except Turnbull, who was drowned.

div.head: ON PLEASURE BENT.
div.p: ON PLEASURE BENT.
KO-KO'S CHAT WITH A BOATMAN.

Avast there, you Warrington jotters. Bring your- selves to an anchor, so to say, and prepare to take in ballast. Your humble servant is for the nonce rusticating in the valley of the Aire, in the throttle nest of 01,1 England, and close alongside as pretty a stretch of water es can be imeginol. None of your .ltlersey muds and stink here,no forges belching black tmoke over Nature's neantiful garb, and no travelling honey pots throwing off tweet odours in (lie oi wet. Right away out ia he country, listen- ing to the twittering of the birds, and watching the course of love's young dream in the shape of fond lovers loitering on the opposite bank of the river, Ko-Ku is indeed himself again. To tell the truth, Iliad forgotten your grimy, busy neighbour- hotel altogether, until I happened scrota a tablet of "Perfection -when taking my matutinal tub. Thus reminded, I net to work on a serioble. Prim- ary object- to fill up space. Secondary object- -to Fenn alt something for the palates of the readers of the " Examiner." At least that's the way it strikes me. The editor tnay think otherwise. Ile weloonie to do 00. 1 ant on pleasure bent, and I take dictation from no one 11124 now—except, per- haps, it be you, ladies and gentlemen. Indeed, I have not much to say, list I can give you the bene- fit of a little chat I've just been having with a boatman. If you don't Care about it you Can stop off right here. The space will be filled, all the

I TM river these holidays has been tilled with I small craft, and now, when the crosh is over, I find 1! myself mulling through tire water in solitary pos- Illes-eton.ym rather a dab baud will; lire oars,and can also navigate a canoe, perhaps as well as Mr. Peers I sails Inc boat on the lereity,and whim I pull at, at I the lauding stage I drop easily into conversation with the old chap who draws shekels for the hire of Iris boats. Ile iv a true specimen of the village Yorkshireman. blunt but kindly ; not very learned. perhaps. but none the less intelligent. 11is broad vernacular I cannot give. If I did you couldn't understand it, so what's Ow odds? Have you ever noticed the temerity of people who take a canoe f..r the first time? They will scramble into a cockle- shell snit of a skiff without any fear, to the itamtn- ont peril ot their livas, but a canoe they consider attogeth;era more dangerous thing. This is just where they make a mistake. Appearances not- . withstanding, a well built. and not too narrow canoe is gaite ILA safe as an ordinary skiff, and much more so than some of them. My friend the boat- - man explained that lie had canoes and canoes. One, rather tubbish in look, was devoted to the use of learners, and by degrees tne canoes got narrower ! and narrower, so that after, as it were, taking the • series, one can become a finished hand at the business. . . . .

.... „ People who !are these boats, however, are not always as modest as you and 1, and the boatman now and again gets deceived. A yottog fellow, say a clerk or a shopman from Bradford or Leeds, will ' come swaggering up "to have a row, don't you know," and make it out that he has been used to l the water all his life. The chances are that he has l been once, and only once, on the bosom of the l treacherous ocean in the neighbourhood of More- cowls- Bay, or Blackpool, and on the small know- ledge thus obtained be presumes too much. There's no bottling such people back, so the boatman lets I him have the pick of the boats. Of course he takes, by instinct, the most unsafe of all the craft, and occasionally the result is that his nibs finds himself sprawling in the dampness. " What do you 40 then," lash? "Fish him out wi this crook' the reply. as my newly-formed acquaintance produces along pole with some twisted iron at the end which he uses to steady the boats as they depart from and arrive at the landing stage. I "We've only bad one drowning case hen.," he con- , tinues, and by way of draining him out I remarked that that was most probably due to ,arelessness. I "Whiskey "woo the laconic answer. " You see there's a public-house just below here, and after haying had something to sup there, a party of , chaps set off with a pint bottle of whiskey in the l boat. Before they'd gone far one of them, in a lark, tried to keep the bottle to himself, and another, who sat at the opposite end of the boat, tried to take it from him. Somehow, all the weight got at otw end, the water came in, and the boat tipped up and sank. My two lads went to them with boats. and I can on the side of the field with the crook, and we picked four of them out. They went away, land soon afterwards found that one of the party was missing. Ile had gone down and stopped then., and his mates ditrnt know but what be was mined, ao you can think how they wen," , Pretty dross, I thought. but I'd scarcely time to i say so before the ancient mariner ran off at a tangent to narrate how once, when a party were afloat to land after a row, the boat capsixed. One of the occupants was a woman who carried in her arms a bairn of about six months old, and, although her head was under water, sloe held the yooing one up with one arm until both wee' saved. , 1 thowt it wur a noble trick;' he said, as a tear i or two glistened in Ids honest eyes at the recollec- I tion. And so it was. How many of us would have hail the presence of mind to do the same? We eller an for some time longer, the boatman and 1, and I l leave the sold boy with the conviction that be is a jolly good fellow, and that boating is rattling good exercise. If the Mersey wasn't to Restestably nasty, I should like to advocate a lot more boating. For I those who do not CAM for crieketing honours, and l who have some sort of contempt for lawn tennis, croquet, and the like, boating is just the thing. I Th,. exercise if+ healthy, not two violent, and is plea- . sant - bar the stink in the case of the Mersey. 1 l have heard that there is, or was, a rowing club at Warrington, but if it is still in existence one does not hear much of its doings. I know there are boats to he hired Wilderspool way, and should like to see them oftener used.
arrington people are getting pretty well used to the Mersey now. They promenade its banks, ' '

some are even venturesome enough to bathe in its waters. so that, putting the question of olfactory sensitiveness on one side. I don't see why boating should not become far more popular locally than it is now. The danger is very small, given proper prudence, but of course, now that the baths are well supplied with water, everybody will soon know how to swim, and if they happen to get in,' they can get out again. , I stank that is about all at present. I shall be j down your way again soon just to put local affairs in order. Until then, adieu.
